transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: The Hive Blight [H-02], Gullet Ford [L-01].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain needles the reeds as you come down the last muddy slope to Gullet Ford, where the Sallow runs waist-deep and fast between rotted banks. A sunken cart lists in the current, its ribs black with algae, half-blocking the shallowest crossing. Reed banks rise tall on both sides — good cover for anyone who doesn't want to be seen crossing, or for anyone waiting to see who tries. Somewhere under the churn, the old ferry-line still sags between two posts, and the far bank is just a smear of grey through the downpour. This is the only dry road south for miles, and it does not look dry today.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The water's higher than yesterday and running faster. Let me see what's safe to cross—and what might be waiting in those reeds.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra moves to the ford's edge, rain needling her face. She crouches to study the churn and speed of the water, reading the marks on the banks and the way the current shifts around the sunken cart. She listens, too—the way a bell-ringer listens—for what the flood's rising rhythm is telling her. Her eyes track the reed banks for movement and signs of ambush.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I'll check it first. If the blight's in that water, it won't hide from me.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm immediately strides to the ford's edge and kneels in the mud, studying the churning current, the sunken cart, and the reed banks for any sign of infected movement or the subtle wrongness that clings to hive-touched places.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: The cart's the trap, not the blessing. Current hits hard on the right side where it lists. We go left where those reeds bend all the same way—shallower tongue there, and more stable footing.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock moves to the water's edge, crouching low to study the ford's current. She reads the churning around the sunken cart, traces the flow with one hand, watches how the reeds bend in the wind-shear. Years of swamp crossings—some made bringing laboring women to safety in worse—teach her where the current is honest and where it lies.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: There—the shallower run to the west, where the reeds thin. We can ford there one at a time and use that sunken wood for cover if we need it. The current's mean but it won't take us if we're quick and careful.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow crouches at the muddy bank, letting the rain needle his shoulders as he studies the churning water. His eyes trace the current's pattern around the sunken cart, mark where the reed banks thin and open, read the angle of that old ferry-line still straining between its posts. Brack pads to his side, her marsh-hound nostrils flaring as she tastes the dampness. Years as a Weir-Keeper taught him to read water the way other men read faces.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — overcome with Notice: dice - 0 - -, invoking Ear for reading water levels and weather [PE-01], Can read the flood's rising rhythm [PE-03] → Superb (+5) vs Good (+3): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — overcome with Investigate: dice + 0 + + → Fantastic (+6) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — create advantage with Notice: dice + 0 + +, invoking Unshakeable calm in any birth, any storm [CA-04] → Epic (+7) vs Good (+3): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice - + 0 + → Superb (+5) vs Good (+3): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Between the four of you, Gullet Ford gives up its secrets. Petra reads the current's rising rhythm and marks exactly where the flood will bite next; Anselm wades in close enough to be sure — no wrongness in the water, no hive-taint on the wind here, just cold honest river. Caddock's steady hand traces the safe tongue of shallows left of the wreck, calling it with a midwife's unshakeable certainty, and Yarrow finds the western run where the reeds thin, Brack's ears pricked for anything moving in the green. Between Caddock's read and Yarrow's, you've got it mapped clean: a path through the shallows that avoids the cart's grasping current and keeps you out of easy ambush line from the banks. The crossing that looked like a coin-flip an hour ago is now something you could walk blind. Whatever's waiting on the far side, at least the ford itself won't be what kills you today.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: You go in one at a time, Petra calling the rhythm of the water like a countdown, Caddock guiding hands and feet along the shallow tongue past the wreck's black ribs. The current tugs hard at the knees, cold enough to steal breath, but the line holds. Reeds hiss and lean on both banks, thick enough to hide a dozen watchers, and twice you catch movement that might be birds. By the time the last of you claws up the far bank, soaked and shaking, Hollowmoot's smoke-haze smudges the grey sky ahead — closer now than it's ever felt.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Everyone whole? We made it clean.  Listen—do you hear that, or is it just me?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra pulls herself up the far bank, her apprentice's clothes streaming water. She runs a wet hand through her hair and immediately turns back toward the others, counting heads—Anselm, Caddock, Yarrow—all accounted for. Her breathing slows into the rhythm that comes with listening. Her head tilts slightly, as if she's hearing something the others can't yet. The swarm-song seems distant but present, like a bell tolling from far across the marsh.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That smoke—it carries hive-taint, I can read it in the way the wind shies from it. We're not getting warmer standing here, and neither is the blight. We move toward it now.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm strips water from his sleeves in sharp, purposeful motions, his eyes already locked on Hollowmoot's murk ahead. He's checking his salt and herbs, letting his fingers brush the small carved tokens of Saint Orrin he carries—old signs against what's coming. He turns to press forward toward the smoke, not waiting.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Everyone's accounted for? No twisted ankles from that current? Those reeds—I didn't like the movement in them, and it wasn't just wind through the stalks.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock reaches back to steady the last person up the slippery bank, her midwife's trained eyes already scanning everyone for shock or injury. She turns to look back across the ford, watching the reed banks with the wariness of someone who knows the marsh's secrets. Her hand rests on her pack straps, ready.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: That crossing held better than it had any right to. But Hollowmoot's closer now, and I don't like how quiet these reeds have gotten.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow hauls himself up the muddy bank and wrings the icy water from his cloak, his breath coming hard. He turns back to watch the others clear the far side, then turns toward Hollowmoot's smoke-smudged horizon ahead, hand resting on his thigh. He takes in the reeds, the ground, the direction of the wind—reading the marsh like a map.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The ford gives up nothing more than cold water and cramped legs. No hooked spear breaks from the reeds, no cry goes up from the wreck's shadow — whatever watched you cross, it let you pass. You come up the far bank soaked, shaking, whole. Ahead, Hollowmoot's smoke-haze thickens against the grey sky, and under it, faint as a memory of a bell, the swarm-song threads through the rain. Gullet Ford falls behind you now, its reeds and its wreck swallowed by the murk — whatever waits, it waits closer, in the smoke.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Tam — I delivered her to the Millbrook goat-herders the year before the fire. She was one of only three children I saved from the burning. I raised her as my own daughter. Last spring she tried crossing alone seeking medicine for the fever in our camp, and Tallow's toll-debt caught her. She's been missing since.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: 'For the greater good' — those are the words that burned Marrowreed and orphaned Tam. I will not hear them again, not for her debt, not for anything.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Last of Marrowreed Village'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: Old Tallow the toll-warden shoulders through the reeds, a waterlogged ledger clutched to his chest, and jabs a swollen finger at a faded line of ink — 'debts written in ledgers don't wash out, not even in eleven years of rain,' he says, and reads a name owed a crossing that the ledger will not forgive. begs the party to go to He begs the party to go to the burned ruins of Marrowreed Village, where the last handful of survivors Caddock knows by name have made a hidden camp among the ash., because her son followed the swarm-song into the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Old Tallow doesn't wait for an answer. He turns the ledger so Caddock can see the ink himself — a name, a date, a crossing never paid for — and behind him the reeds shiver as two Warden toll-men wade closer, spears low but ready. Beyond them, north along the burned tree-line, smoke that isn't cook-smoke rises thin and grey over what's left of Marrowreed: the survivors' hidden camp, where Tam should be — if the fever hasn't already carried her under, or the swarm-song hasn't called her son into the drowned belltower and left her chasing him. The rain keeps coming, patient as the ledger, patient as the debt it will not forgive. Every step toward the ash now is a step deeper into Tallow's book, and a step further from the safe road back to Hollowmoot.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Master Tallow, I know what the ledger writes, and it doesn't wash out. Your boy followed the swarm-song into the belltower—we hear it too. Tell us the debt, tell us the name, and we'll help you settle it.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward with hands visible and open, moving slowly past the spear-men. She's lived at the Ashwater Tollgate her whole life—she knows the language of debts and ledgers, and she respects it completely. She looks directly at Old Tallow, meeting the desperation in his eyes with steady, practical calm.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Your boy followed the swarm-song into that belltower, didn't he? That ledger doesn't matter anymore, Tallow—the hive's got him now, and it's spreading. Let us pass, or I'll move through you both.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward through the rain, body tense and ready, hand dropping toward his belt. He plants himself between Tallow and the rest of the party, eyes hard and certain—the look of an exorcist who has seen hive-touched and survived them. He's not asking to pass. He's stating what will happen next.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Your son went into that song, and Tam chased fever into debt—both of us know loss written in ways the rain can't wash out. I'm going to Marrowreed. Let's save who we can.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock turns toward the burned tree-line where the survivors' camp smokes, her bearing steady as a midwife facing a hard labor. The toll-men's spears don't make her hesitate. She knows grief when she sees it, and she knows the only answer Tallow has left is the same one she has: forward, into the ash, toward whoever might still be saved.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Old Tallow, I know the weight of a promise owed. But you came all this way to tell us her name, not to block the ford — your son's in that belltower, following the swarm-song. You need us to go into Marrowreed more than you need to collect this debt right now.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward into the space between Caddock and Tallow, hands open and empty, boots planted in the mud. His eyes go to the ledger, then to the toll-men's spears, then back to Tallow's face — he's seen that look before, the look of a man trying to hold something together with anger and ink. He doesn't flinch from the spear-points.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Four voices land on Old Tallow at once — Petra's steady respect for the ledger, Anselm's blunt threat, Caddock's grief meeting grief, Yarrow's plain reading of what Tallow actually needs. It's the last that breaks him: his shoulders drop, the ledger sags in his arms, and behind him the toll-men's spears dip toward the mud without an order given. 'Go,' Tallow rasps, wiping rain or something else from his face. 'Bring back whoever's left. The debt — the debt can wait on the dead to settle it.' He doesn't move from the ford as you pass, just stands there clutching his book like it might still write him a better ending. Ahead, the burned tree-line of Marrowreed smokes thin and grey, and under the rain you can just hear it — the swarm-song, patient, pulling toward the belltower.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The mud gives way to timber as you climb the slick ladders into Hollowmoot, stilt-houses leaning shoulder to shoulder over black water, smoke-haze thick enough to taste. Word of the crossing has beaten you here — a runner must have poled ahead — because eyes track you window to window, and the town's toll-keeper meets you at the first walkway with Tallow's ledger already open, your names half-written in it. Behind her, thin and constant under the rain, the swarm-song threads out from the drowned temple's belltower, and more than one Hollowmoot face turns toward it and then quickly away. Somewhere south, smoke that isn't cook-smoke still rises over what's left of Marrowreed. You have until dusk to find a dry hearth, or the doors bar and you're left to the reeds and whatever's listening to that bell.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The ledger's due, I know. But that bell's singing wrong. Is anyone up there ringing it, or is it calling on its own?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (I step forward respectfully toward the toll-keeper and her ledger, acknowledging the crossing's price. But my eyes and ears turn to the belltower as the swarm-song threads through the rain and smoke—I tilt my head, listening hard, trying to read what the bell is actually calling.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Save the ledger—that's hive-song pouring from the belltower. I need to know what's singing it before dusk locks us in here.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps past the toll-keeper without waiting, his scarred hands already moving to the herbs and charms woven through his belt, checking his tools and remedies. His gaze is locked on the smoke-hazed outline of the drowned temple's belltower, where the swarm-song threads thin and constant beneath the rain.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Mirel, is it? I know how the ledger works. But that smoke south—that's where I'm from. What's burning at Marrowreed, and what's that song coming from the temple?

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock climbs into Hollowmoot with the others, noting the watching eyes and the ledger-bearing toll-keeper. But her gaze pulls toward the smoke rising over Marrowreed—her home. She greets Mirel with the respect owed to a toll-keeper, but asks direct questions about what's burning and what that constant bell-song means.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Tallow sent word we're squared at the ford. What does Hollowmoot want from us to keep shelter and keep moving come dawn?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward to meet Mirel's eyes directly, his posture easy and his hands visible. His gaze shifts between the toll-keeper, the ledger already half-filled with their names, and the town itself—tracking the swarm-song's thin thread rising from the drowned temple, the smoke rising south over Marrowreed's burned ruins, counting the watching faces in the windows above. He's looking for where the real danger lives in Hollowmoot, and for Brack.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That bell is singing with hive-voice—nothing else matters until I know what's ringing it. Your ledger can wait.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm doesn't wait for Mirel's ledger or anyone's leave — he shoulders past her toward the walkway that angles south to the temple causeway, herbs and charms already in hand, eyes fixed on the belltower. Mirel's mouth thins; she doesn't chase him, but she draws a line through the half-written name and marks something else beside it instead, murmuring "debt unanswered" to the toll-man at her shoulder. The swarm-song, thin and constant, seems to catch on Anselm's sudden movement — for one breath it stutters, then thickens, like something on the far end of that sound just noticed a listener who actually knows what he's hearing. Petra feels it too, a wrongness under the rhythm she can't yet name. Mirel turns back to the three who remain, weighing them now against the one who walked off: to Petra's question about the bell she only shrugs — "No one's climbed that tower in years, and it still rings" — but to Caddock's question about Marrowreed her face goes carefully blank, and she says only that the Wardens "cleared" it three days past, no more. To Yarrow she's plainer: Hollowmoot doesn't bar its doors on strangers who've paid and behaved, and right now the ledger says this party hasn't finished either.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: The bell caught you, Anselm—something's listening now from that tower. I'm coming with you.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's body goes rigid as the swarm-song thickens and shifts beneath the rain-sound. She calls out sharply, her voice cutting across the walkway with the clarity of a bell-ringer's apprentice who can hear what others miss. Without waiting for Mirel's ledger-mark or anyone's leave, she moves immediately to follow Anselm toward the causeway—because she's the only one here who can hear that listening on the far end of the bell, and that means she needs to be where he is when it decides to pull.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: That bell heard me listening. I'm climbing that tower before dusk seals the doors—if Saint Orrin's Tongue is ringing there, I need it before the hive claims it.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm pushes along the slick walkways toward the temple causeway, moving with the urgency of someone who hears a predator calling his name. Scarred hands check the herbs and charms woven through his belt as he navigates the stilt-town's narrow paths. He's listening hard past the swarm-song's hypnotic rhythm, tuning for the deeper note underneath—trying to hear whether it's Saint Orrin's Tongue singing beneath the hive-voice or something that's wrapped hive-taint around the tower's ancient bell like a living skin. The belltower looms through the smoke-haze ahead, and the swarm-song pulses with awareness.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I hear you, Mirel. The Wardens cleared Marrowreed, and that's a grief I'll carry. But right now—that bell is singing hive-song, and my friend just walked toward it alone. What does Hollowmoot need from us to keep shelter and keep breathing until dawn?

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock's hands stay steady as the words settle into her. Her gaze meets Mirel's with the direct respect owed to a toll-keeper, but her eyes keep tracking the path Anselm took toward the temple's belltower, where that swarm-song threads thin and wrong under the rain. She's not broken by what she's just learned about her home—she's centered. Professional. Focused on what the group needs to survive the night.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: I hear you. What does Hollowmoot's ledger show we owe here, and what does 'finished' mean — a crossing toll, a night's shelter, something else?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow keeps his hands visible and his posture easy, showing he's not looking for trouble. While he speaks to Mirel, his eyes track the walkway Anselm took toward the temple, counting the watching faces in the windows around them, and searching through the smoke-haze for any sign of Brack. He's learned to work within the Warden structure even after his disgrace — respect the ledger, know your obligations, pay what's owed.)

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: No—no, that's not— I'm coming, Anselm! I'm coming!

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts a compel.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — overcome with Investigate: dice + 0 + -, invoking Reads the ruined liturgy others can't [AN-03] → Fantastic (+6) vs Great (+4): SUCCESS

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Anselm plants himself at the causeway's edge, forcing the hive-song's pulse into pieces the way the old liturgy trained him to — and underneath the wrongness, he finds structure. This isn't a swarm keening at random. It's Saint Orrin's own bell-pattern, the Tongue's true ring, dragged through hive-taint like a hymn sung through a drowned throat. Something is ringing it deliberately, or something is wearing the ringing like a skin. Petra reaches him just as the recognition hits, and the moment his understanding steadies, she feels the song's rhythm shift toward her — not random anymore, answering, the way her own bell-ringing always seems to answer it. She goes rigid again, her free hand finding the edge of the rail as if to steady herself against a memory of nearly drowning to it. Behind them on the walkway, Caddock and Yarrow hold the line with Mirel, who — seeing two of the party peel off toward the temple unbidden — hardens rather than softens, tapping her ledger meaningfully and warning that Hollowmoot won't shelter debts that walk away from her mid-conversation.

transcript.speaker: Petra

transcript.text: Anselm's counter-liturgy cuts the swarm-song like a blade through wet rope — for three heartbeats the belltower's voice fractures into its true shape, Saint Orrin's own ancient pattern, before the hive-taint swallows it whole again. Petra, gripping the rail beside him, feels the song release its grip on her name the instant Anselm's words land — she gasps like she's surfaced from underwater, shaking but herself again. Behind them, Caddock's answer to Mirel lands harder than she meant it to; the toll-keeper's jaw tightens at "cleared," and she marks something final in the ledger, murmuring that Hollowmoot remembers who asks uncomfortable questions about Warden work. Yarrow holds the line beside Caddock, steady and visible, and it's enough — as dusk's grey deepens toward true dark, Mirel finally closes the ledger with a snap and tips her head toward a leaning stilt-house down the walkway.
